There's a particular kind of silence that happens in a library just after closing time is announced. Not the silence of emptiness—the silence of people deciding. Someone at a far table is weighing whether the paragraph they're on is worth finishing. Someone else is already packing, but slowly, because leaving means admitting the day is over.

I find myself drawn to these threshold moments, the small hinges between one state and the next. The pause before a phone call connects. The half-second when a struck match hasn't yet decided whether to catch. Water at the lip of a glass, right before it spills or doesn't.

What interests me is that these moments are mostly invisible. We remember beginnings and endings; we build ceremonies around them. But the actual crossing, the transition itself, tends to slip past unrecorded. Nobody photographs the instant the train doors begin to close. Nobody writes down the exact moment a conversation stopped being polite and became real.

And yet that's where most of living happens, I suspect. Not in the states themselves but in the movement between them. A friendship isn't a thing you have; it's a thing that keeps becoming. The same with understanding something—there's no moment you finally "get it," only a long series of getting it slightly more.

So I try to notice the hinges. The librarian flicking lights off one row at a time. The last reader standing, book still open, letting the sentence end on its own terms before she goes.
